name: South Gully
approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (elev. ~3,400 ft) on FS Road 7601 off Icicle Road. Follow the Stuart Lake Trail (Trail #1599) north through Douglas-fir/subalpine forest, crossing Mountaineer Creek on sturdy footbridges; the grade is moderate for the first 2.5 miles (about 1,500 ft gain) to the signed junction with the Colchuck Lake Trail — go left/uphill. From the junction the trail steepens and grows rockier for another 1.5 miles to Colchuck Lake (about 4 miles and ~2,280 ft from the TH, lake at 5,570 ft) — the last reliable, easy water source before the high basin. Boulder-hop/skirt the lake's south shore to the base of Aasgard Pass, a steep, unmaintained talus-and-boulder gully with only faint tread and cairns; it gains roughly 2,000–2,200 ft in under 1.25 miles to the pass (~7,800–7,841 ft) — this is the single biggest approach hazard on the route: loose, shifting rock with real rockfall risk onto parties below, and in early season the gully holds snow/ice that turns it into a steep, exposed snow climb. From the pass, drop gently into the upper Enchantment core basin past Isolation Lake, then traverse cross-country (use-paths and cairns, no maintained trail) through the Tranquil/Perfection/Sigrun/Reginleif lakes tarn cluster toward the Enchantment Peak massif; this route leaves the basin directly between Lake Reginleif and Lake Sigrun and climbs talus to the gully on the peak's south side below the northeast summit, avoiding the longer detour via Prusik Pass. This upper section is class 2–3 talus and slab with sustained exposure in spots; snow lingering into summer can make it markedly harder and is best avoided when icy (some parties instead take the longer, mellower line via Prusik Pass in spring conditions). The route enters fragile alpine terrain in the wilderness's day-use/permit core zone — stay on rock or snow and avoid cutting across meadow or heather. One-way distance to the summit is roughly 7.5–8 miles with about 5,100 ft of net rise from trailhead to summit; counting the drop into the basin and the reclimb to Aasgard Pass on the way out, the round trip comes to roughly 6,650 ft of gain for a car-to-car push (long day; many split it with a camp near Colchuck or in the core zone under permit).

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the core basin to the south side
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead on FS Road 7601. Stuart Lake Trail #1599 north through forest, crossing Mountaineer Creek on footbridges, moderate for the first 2.5 miles to the signed Colchuck Lake junction — go left and uphill. Steeper and rockier for another 1.5 miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. That is the last easy water before the high basin.

Skirt the lake's south shore to the foot of Aasgard Pass and climb the pass: roughly 2,000-2,200 ft in under 1.25 miles on faint tread, cairns, loose talus and boulders.

Aasgard has one route-finding rule that matters more than any other and it has killed people. A few hundred feet above the lake the path veers to the climber's left of the creek. Keep left. At the first grove of larches, stay well clear to the left of the rock, whatever the season. At around 6,400 ft stay left of the small cliff band with the waterfall in it, and do not follow any side path toward the waterfall. Drifting right of the trees, toward the waterfall ground, is how parties get cliffed out.

From the pass drop gently into the upper core basin past Isolation Lake and traverse cross-country on use-paths and cairns through the Tranquil / Perfection / Sigrun / Reginleif tarns toward the Enchantment Peak massif. This route leaves the basin directly between Lake Reginleif and Lake Sigrun and climbs talus onto the peak's south side, toward the gully below the northeast summit.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun to early Oct snow-free; Apr-Jun normally needs an ice axe for Aasgard Pass and the upper basin
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose shifting rock and genuine rockfall risk onto parties below
Getting cliffed out right of the trees / near the waterfall band at ~6,400 ft — fatalities are on record there
Early-season snow and ice turning the pass into a steep exposed snow climb
Sustained exposure on the class 2-3 talus and slab above the basin, worse when snow lingers
Fragile alpine ground in the permit core zone — stay on rock or snow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The scrambling starts where the basin talus steepens onto the peak's south flank — there is no cliff base, just a change of angle, so the useful test is about the summit rather than the start.

This route finishes on the northeast summit: class 2-3 ground and a short third-class finish onto a small flat block, which a 2023 survey found to be six or seven feet higher than the southwest summit. The southwest summit, roughly 1,500 ft away along the crest, is a very exposed fourth-class scramble and is not part of this route — if the crest ahead turns into sustained, exposed fourth-class ground, you have gone past your summit.

On the way in, the marker that you have left the basin at the right place is the pair of lakes: the line goes between Lake Reginleif and Lake Sigrun onto the south side. If you are heading for Prusik Pass you have taken the longer, mellower option, which is a reasonable choice in spring conditions but does not lead to this scramble.
